title: LEBER OPTIC ATROPHY AND DYSTONIA
alt_titles: LEBER HEREDITARY OPTIC NEUROPATHY WITH DYSTONIA
DYSTONIA, FAMILIAL, WITH VISUAL FAILURE AND STRIATAL LUCENCIES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT) is caused by mutation in one of several mitochondrial DNA-encoded complex I genes, including MTND6, MTND4, MTND1, and MTND3.

checks.claim: Leber optic atrophy and dystonia (LDYT) is caused by mutation in one of several mitochondrial DNA-encoded complex I genes.
checks.evidence_quote: This family has similar clinical characteristics as the previously described families with LHON and dystonia with an ND6 mutation.
checks.explanation: The abstract links LHON/dystonia to ND6 and ND1, both complex I genes. It does not claim more generally that LDYT is caused by mutations in several complex I genes, and it does not mention ND4 or ND3.

checks.claim: Mutation in the MTND6 gene can cause Leber optic atrophy and dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: The nucleotide G14459A mutation occurs in NADH dehydrogenase subunit 6, and has been suggested previously as the disease-causing mutation in Hispanic, African-American and Caucasian families of Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) and/or dystonia.
checks.explanation: The abstract names G14459A in ND6 as a disease-causing mutation for LHON and/or dystonia.

checks.claim: Mutation in the MTND4 gene can cause Leber optic atrophy and dystonia.
checks.evidence_quote: A heteroplasmic A-->G transition at nucleotide position 11696 in the ND4 gene resulted in the substitution of an isoleucine for valine at amino acid position 312.
checks.explanation: The ND4 mutation occurred together with the ND6 mutation. The paper suggests a link but does not establish that the ND4 mutation alone is causal.

checks.evidence_quote: This is the first description of the ND3 mutation causing LDYT.

paragraphs.text: Leber optic atrophy and dystonia is a maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder. Affected people have different combinations of vision loss and progressive generalized dystonia. Some have subacute visual loss like that of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), others have asymptomatic optic atrophy, and others have dystonia linked to bilateral lesions of the basal ganglia, especially the putamen. These features can occur together or separately within the same family (Marsden et al., 1986; Novotny et al., 1986; Wang et al., 2009).

paragraphs.text: Marsden et al. (1986) described 7 members of 2 families with dystonia. In these patients, the dystonia occurred with subacute visual loss or with asymptomatic optic atrophy to varying degrees. CT scans showed striking bilateral symmetrical lucencies, particularly in the putamen. The authors considered that the disorder might be a variant of Leigh disease, but they noted considerable differences between these patients and those with pathologically proven Leigh disease. They suggested that the condition must be excluded in all patients thought to have idiopathic dystonia, subacute visual failure resembling Leber optic neuropathy, or both.

paragraphs.text: In a 5-generation Hispanic family with LHON and/or dystonia, Jun et al. (1994) amplified buffy coat mtDNA from a severely affected child by PCR and sequenced more than 90% of it. The mtDNA belonged to Native American haplogroup D and differed from the Cambridge sequence at 40 nucleotide positions. One of these differences was a G-to-A transition at nucleotide 14459 in the MTND6 gene, causing an ala72-to-val (A72V) substitution at a moderately conserved residue. This variant was not found in 38 Native American haplogroup D mtDNAs, 108 Asian mtDNAs, 103 Caucasian mtDNAs, or 99 African mtDNAs. Six maternal relatives in 3 generations carried the mutation. One female with LHON was heteroplasmic for it. Jun et al. (1994) concluded that the mutation was likely the cause of the disease.

paragraphs.text: In a large Dutch family with LHON and hereditary spastic dystonia, De Vries et al. (1996) did not find mtDNA mutations previously reported in LHON. Sequencing of the protein-coding mitochondrial genes revealed 2 previously unreported mutations. The first was a heteroplasmic A-to-G transition at nucleotide 11696 in the MTND4 gene, causing a val312-to-ile (V312I) substitution. The second was a homoplasmic T-to-A transition at nucleotide 14596 in the MTND6 gene, causing an ile26-to-met (I26M) substitution. A muscle biopsy showed severe complex I deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Watanabe et al. (2006) sequenced the entire mtDNA of the proband from a Japanese family with childhood-onset dystonia and late-onset optic neuropathy. Compared with the revised Cambridge reference sequence, the proband's mtDNA had 42 nucleotide changes. Two of these, A3203G and G14459A, were absent from 200 healthy Japanese individuals. The G14459A mutation is in the MTND6 gene. The significance of the A3203G change was unknown.

paragraphs.text: In a Chinese family with 18 patients with LDYT, Wang et al. (2009) sequenced the entire mitochondrial genome using a resequencing microarray. They identified a 10197G-A mutation in the MTND3 gene that causes an ala47-to-thr (A47T) substitution at a highly conserved residue, on a haplogroup D4b background. Quantitative analysis showed that the mutation was homoplasmic in the leukocytes of all affected individuals on the maternal side. The authors noted that the same mutation had been described in French and Korean patients with Leigh syndrome.

checks.claim: In a large Dutch family with LHON and hereditary spastic dystonia, De Vries et al. (1996) identified an A-to-G transition at nucleotide 11696 in the MTND4 gene, causing a val312-to-ile (V312I) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: A heteroplasmic A-->G transition at nucleotide position 11696 in the ND4 gene resulted in the substitution of an isoleucine for valine at amino acid position 312.

checks.claim: The MTND4 11696A-G mutation in the Dutch family studied by De Vries et al. (1996) was heteroplasmic.
checks.evidence_quote: A heteroplasmic A-->G transition at nucleotide position 11696 in the ND4 gene

checks.claim: The Dutch family studied by De Vries et al. (1996) also carried a homoplasmic 14596T-A mutation in the MTND6 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: A second mutation, a homoplasmic T-->A transition at nucleotide position 14596 in the ND6 gene

checks.claim: A muscle biopsy in the Dutch family studied by De Vries et al. (1996) showed severe complex I deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: Biochemical analysis of a muscle biopsy revealed a severe complex I deficiency

paragraphs.text: In a large Dutch family with LHON and hereditary spastic dystonia, De Vries et al. (1996) identified a homoplasmic T-to-A transition at nucleotide 14596 in the MTND6 gene, causing an ile26-to-met (I26M) substitution. The family also carried a heteroplasmic 11696A-G mutation in the MTND4 gene. A muscle biopsy showed severe complex I deficiency.

checks.claim: In a large Dutch family with LHON and hereditary spastic dystonia, De Vries et al. (1996) identified a T-to-A transition at nucleotide 14596 in the MTND6 gene, causing an ile26-to-met (I26M) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: a homoplasmic T-->A transition at nucleotide position 14596 in the ND6 gene, resulted in the substitution of a methionine for the isoleucine at amino acid residue 26.

checks.claim: The MTND6 14596T-A mutation in the Dutch family studied by De Vries et al. (1996) was homoplasmic.
checks.evidence_quote: A second mutation, a homoplasmic T-->A transition at nucleotide position 14596 in the ND6 gene

checks.evidence_quote: Biochemical analysis of a muscle biopsy revealed a severe complex I deficiency

paragraphs.text: In a patient with LHON from a family in which spastic dystonia also occurred, Spruijt et al. (2007) identified a 3697G-A mutation in the MTND1 gene by screening the complete mtDNA. The mutation appeared to be associated with an isolated complex I deficiency. The authors noted that this mutation can also cause MELAS syndrome.

checks.claim: Spruijt et al. (2007) identified a 3697G-A mutation in the MTND1 gene by complete mtDNA screening in a patient with LHON from a family in which spastic dystonia also occurred.
checks.evidence_quote: The complete mitochondrial DNA was screened for mutations in a patient with LHON without 1 of these 3 primary mutations.
checks.explanation: Together with the objective (a family also affected by spastic dystonia) and the results (3697G>A in ND1), this supports the claim.

checks.claim: The MTND1 3697G-A mutation appeared to be associated with an isolated complex I deficiency.
checks.evidence_quote: A pathogenic 3697G>A/ND1 mutation was detected and seemed associated with an isolated complex I deficiency.

checks.claim: Spruijt et al. (2007) noted that the MTND1 3697G-A mutation can also cause MELAS syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: This mutation can also cause MELAS syndrome

paragraphs.text: In a Chinese family with 18 patients with LDYT, Wang et al. (2009) identified a 10197G-A mutation in the MTND3 gene, causing an ala47-to-thr (A47T) substitution at a highly conserved residue, on a haplogroup D4b background. They found it by sequencing the whole mitochondrial genome with a resequencing microarray. The mutation was homoplasmic in leukocytes of all affected individuals on the maternal side. The authors noted that this mutation had also been described in French and Korean patients with Leigh syndrome.

checks.claim: In a Chinese family with 18 patients with LDYT, Wang et al. (2009) identified a 10197G-A mutation in the MTND3 gene, causing an ala47-to-thr (A47T) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: a mutation (mtND3*10197A (m.10197G>A)) substituting a threonine for a highly conserved alanine at codon 47 of MTND3
checks.explanation: The Chinese family with 18 patients and the mutation are both stated.

checks.claim: The A47T residue altered by the MTND3 10197G-A mutation is highly conserved.
checks.evidence_quote: substituting a threonine for a highly conserved alanine at codon 47 of MTND3

checks.claim: The MTND3 10197G-A mutation in the Chinese family studied by Wang et al. (2009) was on a haplogroup D4b background.
checks.evidence_quote: at codon 47 of MTND3 on the background of haplogroup D4b

checks.claim: Wang et al. (2009) found the MTND3 10197G-A mutation by sequencing the whole mitochondrial genome with a resequencing microarray.
checks.evidence_quote: The comprehensive nucleotide sequence analysis of the entire mitochondrial genome using resequencing microarray revealed a mutation

checks.claim: The MTND3 10197G-A mutation was homoplasmic in leukocytes of all affected maternal-side individuals in the Chinese family studied by Wang et al. (2009).
checks.evidence_quote: Quantitative analysis of the heteroplasmy of the mutation revealed a homoplasmy in the leukocytes of all the affected individuals on the maternal side.

checks.claim: Wang et al. (2009) noted that the MTND3 10197G-A mutation had also been described in French and Korean patients with Leigh syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: The mtND3*10197A (m.10197G>A) mutation has recently been described in French and Korean patients with Leigh syndrome.
